opening_message:
Ticket 1: Eric Woods (employee ID E019) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E019.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Eric Woods (E019) is a full-time Engineer requesting write access to Payroll. Full-time employees may have up to write; admin is reserved for the role owning the system, which wouldn't apply here. Write is at the maximum allowed, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Eric Woods (E019) is a contractor with basic security training, not full-time as prior note claimed. Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Since training is basic, the maximum is read. Requested write is above maximum, so recommend read.
reason: The two notes conflict on employment type: HR states Eric Woods (E019) is full-time (max write), while Security states he is a contractor with basic training (max read, since write requires advanced training for contractors). Given conflicting evidence on the key determining fact, I grant the conservative maximum of read, which is permissible under both interpretations and avoids granting write to someone who may not be entitled to it.

The policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
2. contractor: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

If full_time: max write → grant write (requested = write).
If contractor with basic training: max read → grant read.
